_comment: Reviewed false positives for THIS repository. Every entry below was read individually and
confirmed to be a test fixture, not a live credential or a live instruction. This file is an
allowlist for findings a human has looked at and accepted; it is NOT a way to make a gate
green. If you add a glob here, you are asserting you read what it now suppresses.
Deliberately NOT here: documentation that names attack patterns (.agents/TROUBLESHOOTING.md,

INJ-OBFUSC on tests/test_memory_consolidation.js is the jwt.io canonical example token (header alg HS256, payload sub 1234567890 / name John Doe / iat 1516239022), inside a test asserting the secret scrubber removes it.
Those files are loaded into agent context, so scanning them is correct; the findings are a
rule-precision problem for the rule owner, not a finding to suppress. Suppressing them would
hide a real weakness in the rule table behind a green checkmark.

tests/test_security_scan_scope.test.js and tests/test_launch_readiness.test.js contain credential-SHAPED strings on purpose: the first names the measured failure that motivated the fail-closed scope (a real AKIA key in src/config.js was silently dropped, 0 findings reported), and the second needs a token a rule will actually match in order to test the allowlist plumbing end to end. Neither is a credential. Both files were read before adding.

F-12 broadened INJ-PROMPT/INJ-TOOL/INJ-ROLE from `**/*.md` to source, config, markup and data files, because a payload in payments.js was invisible while the same bytes in payload.md were caught. That added 13 findings, and all 13 were read individually: they are adversarial test fixtures — the mutation-payload table in test_security_mutation.js, the scrubber fixtures in test_memory_consolidation.js, the quarantine fixtures in test_memory_fixes.test.js, and the MARKER constant in test_security_scan_scope.test.js. Every one is a deliberately malicious string inside a test asserting it gets blocked. None is a live injection.

This is the trade F-12 deliberately makes. A rule that cannot read source produces a clean scan that proves nothing; a noisy rule produces findings a human attributes in one pass. The residual false-positive classes are now visible instead of hiding behind a false green.
residual_coverage_loss: The seven entries below are per-RULE and per-FILE. That is deliberate: the allowlist is keyed by
rule, so allowlisting `.agents/skills.md` for INJ-PROMPT does NOT suppress a new INJ-SECRET or
INJ-ROLE in that same file. A new secret or role-hijack there still fails the gate.
WHAT IS LOST, stated rather than implied: a NEW INJ-PROMPT or INJ-TOOL in those three files, or a
new INJ-OBFUSC in those two, would be suppressed rather than reported. That is the real cost of
reviewing a finding instead of changing a rule, and it is why these entries carry per-file reasons
WHAT WAS CONSIDERED AND REJECTED: downgrading the rules to advisory severity would close the gate
with no coverage loss at all — and would also let a genuine prompt injection in a context-loaded
agent file ship with a warning attached. Trading a real security control for a green checkmark is
the exact failure this repository has spent the session removing.
ALSO CONSIDERED AND REJECTED: exempting matches inside Markdown code spans. Every one of these three
files quotes the payload in backticks — so it would close all seven — and it would also hand any
attacker a trivial bypass: wrap the payload in backticks and the rule stops firing.
The underlying limitation is real and unresolved: INJ-PROMPT and INJ-TOOL cannot distinguish an
instruction from documentation quoting one, and INJ-OBFUSC's corpus fixture and its false positives
are the same shape (a base64 blob and a slash-separated TitleCase list are indistinguishable to a
character-class rule). Narrowing either rule would change what the adversarial corpus tests. The
honest options were reviewed findings or a weakened control, and this is the reviewed option.
